title: Is Mimosa Hostilis Dye Colorfast?
summary: On wool and silk, Mimosa hostilis gives colors that hold well in the wash and reasonably well in light, because its tannins bind to protein fiber. Alum mordant improves both, iron-modified greys are the most durable of all, and the pinks are the first shades to soften in strong sun.
body: Colorfast is two questions, not one. **Washfastness** is whether the color survives water, soap and rubbing. **Lightfastness** is whether it survives daylight. A dye can do well on one and poorly on the other, and Mimosa hostilis root bark behaves differently on each.
## Why tannin-rich bark holds its color

Mimosa root bark is heavy with tannins, the same family of compounds that turns hide into leather. Tannins bond to the protein in wool and silk on their own, which is why this bark can dye protein fiber without a separate mordant, and why the color it leaves does not simply rinse out. [What tannins do in a dye bath](/blog/what-tannins-do-in-a-dye-bath) goes into the chemistry.
## Washfastness: good on wool and silk

Once the fiber has cooled in the bath and been rinsed until the water runs clear, the color left behind is well attached. Most dyers find it survives ordinary hand washing without noticeable loss. What does take color out is heat and alkali together: a hot wash with a strongly alkaline detergent will pull the purples toward brown and lift some depth. Wash in cool or lukewarm water with a pH-neutral wool wash, and do not soak for hours.
## Lightfastness: it depends on the shade

The rose, pink and lilac tones are the most delicate part of the range. Hung in a sunny window they soften and warm over months, drifting toward tan. The deeper plums and burgundies last longer simply because there is more dye in the fiber. The slate, grey and charcoal shades that come from an iron afterbath are the most lightfast of all, because the iron and tannin form a dark compound that fades very slowly.

| Shade | How it is made | Light | Wash |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pale rose and lilac | Light bath, or an exhaust bath | Fair: softens in strong sun | Good |
| Plum and burgundy | Heavy bath, 50 to 100% bark | Good | Good |
| Slate and charcoal | Any bath, then an iron afterbath | Very good | Very good |
## How to make the color last longer

- **Mordant with alum first.** Alum at 10 to 15 percent of the dry fiber weight brightens the color and measurably improves how well it holds in light. [Mordanting wool before a bark bath](/blog/mordanting-wool-before-a-bark-bath) gives the method.
- **Dye deep, not pale.** More dye in the fiber means more to lose before you notice a change.
- **Let the fiber cool in the bath.** Taking wool out hot gives the color less time to bond.
- **Rinse until clear.** Loose dye left on the surface is what rubs off onto hands and other clothes.
- **Use iron for the pieces that will see sun.** If a shawl will hang in daylight, the grey end of the range will outlast the pink end.
## Testing your own results

Water, fiber and mordant all change the answer, so the only colorfastness figure that matters is the one from your own pot. For light, cut a dyed swatch in two, keep one half in a drawer and tape the other to a sunny window for two to four weeks, then compare them side by side. For washing, stitch a strip of undyed white cotton to a dyed swatch, wash them together as you would the finished piece, and check the white for staining. [Testing a dye before you commit a fleece](/blog/testing-a-dye-before-you-commit-a-fleece) covers the rest of the sampling routine.
## Cotton and linen

Plant fibers carry no protein, so the tannins have less to hold on to and the color is paler and less durable unless the fiber is mordanted with tannin and then alum before dyeing. With that preparation the results come much closer to wool. [Wool, silk, cotton and linen in the same bath](/blog/wool-silk-cotton-and-linen-in-the-same-bath) shows the difference on one set of swatches.

title: Eco Printing Silk With Mimosa Hostilis Root Bark
summary: To eco print silk with Mimosa hostilis, dye a cotton blanket or the silk itself in a bark bath, lay mordanted leaves on the silk, roll it tightly around a dowel, and steam the bundle for about an hour. The leaves print dark on a plum or rose ground that the bark provides.
body: Eco printing, also called bundle dyeing, transfers the shape and color of leaves straight onto cloth. Leaves are laid on fabric, rolled up tight, and steamed or simmered, and the pigments and tannins in each leaf print where it touched. Mimosa hostilis root bark earns its place in the process as the **background**: it turns the whole scarf a dusky rose or plum, so the leaf prints sit on a colored ground instead of bare white.
## What you need

- A silk scarf or length of silk, washed to remove any finish
- Alum, at 10 to 15 percent of the dry weight of the silk
- Mimosa hostilis root bark: [powder](/product/mimosa-hostilis-root-bark-powder) gives the fastest bath, [shredded](/product/shredded-mimosa-hostilis-root-bark) the cleanest
- Leaves that print well: oak, maple, rose, sumac, eucalyptus and geranium are reliable
- A cotton or silk "blanket" the same size as the silk (optional, for a colored ground)
- A dowel, a length of copper pipe or a smooth stick, and strong string
- A steamer or a large pot with a rack, used only for dyeing
## Step 1: mordant the silk

Dissolve the alum in hot water, add it to a pot of warm water, and soak the wetted silk in it for an hour or more, keeping it below a simmer. Silk marks easily, so do not boil it. Rinse lightly and leave it damp. [Mordanting wool before a bark bath](/blog/mordanting-wool-before-a-bark-bath) uses the same alum percentage.
## Step 2: make the bark bath

For a single scarf, a few tablespoons of powder or a small handful of shredded bark is plenty. Soak it in warm water, bring it to a gentle simmer for 30 to 45 minutes, and strain it well through fine cloth; loose particles of powder will speckle the print. Keep the bath neutral to slightly acidic if you want rose and plum rather than brown. [Filtering a bark bath without losing the colour](/blog/filtering-a-bark-bath-without-losing-the-colour) shows how.
## Step 3: choose how the bark reaches the silk
There are two ways to use the bath, and they give different looks:

- **Blanket method.** Dip the cotton blanket in the bark bath, wring it out, and lay it over the leaves before rolling. The bark color transfers to the silk everywhere except where leaves block it, so the leaves print as crisp shapes with a pale halo on a rose ground.
- **Pre-dyed method.** Dye the silk itself a pale pink in the bath first, then print on it. The leaves print directly onto an even colored ground, with softer edges.
## Step 4: lay out, roll and tie

Spread the damp silk flat and arrange the leaves on half of it, veins down, then fold the other half over (or lay the blanket on top). Roll the whole stack around the dowel as tightly as you can, and bind it hard with string every inch or so. Pressure is what makes a sharp print; a loose bundle gives blurred shapes.
## Step 5: steam or simmer

Steam the bundle for 60 to 90 minutes, turning it once, or simmer it gently in the leftover bark bath for the same time. Then leave it to cool, and if you have patience, leave it wrapped for one to three days. The prints deepen as it rests.
## Step 6: unroll, dry and rest
Unwrap the bundle, shake off the leaves and hang the silk to dry out of the sun. Leave it a week before washing it for the first time, then wash by hand in cool water with a pH-neutral wool wash.
## Getting darker prints

Leaf prints darken dramatically with iron. Dip the blanket in a weak iron solution before rolling, or brush a little onto the leaves, and oak and eucalyptus in particular print near-black on the bark-colored ground. Use iron sparingly on silk, which it can weaken; [iron as a modifier, and how far to go](/blog/iron-as-a-modifier-how-far-to-go) explains how little is enough.
## Common problems

| Problem | Likely cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Speckles on the silk | Powder particles in the bath | Strain through finer cloth, or use shredded bark |
| Blurred leaf shapes | Bundle too loose | Roll tighter and tie every inch |
| Brown ground instead of rose | Alkaline water or too much heat | Keep the bath below a simmer and slightly acidic |
| Faint prints | Leaves too dry, or silk not mordanted | Soak leaves first; mordant with alum |

title: Mimosa Hostilis Compared With Cutch, Oak Gall and Quebracho
summary: Mimosa hostilis, cutch, oak gall and quebracho are all tannin-rich dyes, but they are not interchangeable. Mimosa hostilis is the one for rose, plum and burgundy; cutch gives warm browns, quebracho red-browns, and oak gall is used mainly as a tannin mordant and, with iron, for greys and blacks.
body: Walk into any natural-dye supplier and you will find a shelf of tannin-rich materials: bark, heartwood and galls, all of which bond readily to wool and silk and all of which darken with iron. They are easy to confuse. Here is how Mimosa hostilis root bark compares with the three it is most often weighed against, and when each is the right choice.
## At a glance

| Material | Source | Colors on wool | Main use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mimosa hostilis | Root bark of Mimosa tenuiflora | Rose, plum, burgundy, brown; slate with iron | Pinks and purples from a single material |
| Cutch | Heartwood of Senegalia catechu | Tan, cinnamon, deep brown | Warm browns |
| Quebracho | Heartwood of Schinopsis trees | Pink-tan to red-brown | Red-browns, leather |
| Oak gall | Galls on oak trees | Beige; grey to black with iron | Tannin mordant for cotton and linen |
## Mimosa hostilis: the purple end of the tannins

What sets Mimosa root bark apart is its color. Most tannin dyes give browns and tans; this one gives dusky rose, plum and burgundy on wool and silk, and holds those tones as long as the bath stays neutral to slightly acidic. It needs no separate mordant on protein fiber, gives two or three exhaust baths from one batch, and turns slate to charcoal with an iron afterbath. [Keeping a bark bath purple instead of brown](/blog/keeping-a-bark-bath-purple) is the main skill it asks for.
## Cutch: warm, dependable browns

Cutch comes from the heartwood of the khair tree, and is sold as dark chips, cakes or powder. It is one of the most reliable browns in natural dyeing, from a light cinnamon to near chocolate, and with iron it goes to cool brown-greys. Choose cutch when you want brown and want it predictable. Choose Mimosa hostilis when you want the brown to lean purple, or want pinks from the same pot.
## Quebracho: red-browns, and a leather-trade staple

Red quebracho is the heartwood of South American Schinopsis trees and one of the major tanning materials of the leather industry. On wool it gives pinkish tans through to red-brown. It overlaps with Mimosa hostilis at the brown end, but it does not reach the same clear roses and plums. For leather, both work well; [dyeing leather with bark](/blog/dyeing-leather-with-bark) covers Mimosa bark on vegetable-tanned hides.
## Oak gall: a mordant more than a color

Oak galls are growths on oak trees caused by gall wasps, and they are among the most concentrated tannin sources there are. On their own they give little more than beige, so dyers use them mainly as a **tannin mordant**, soaking cotton and linen in gall solution before alum so plant fibers can take color well. With iron, oak gall gives greys and blacks and is the classic basis of iron-gall ink. It does not compete with Mimosa hostilis for color; it helps other dyes, Mimosa included, take on cotton.
## A note on the name "mimosa"

In the leather trade, "mimosa" tanning material usually means the bark of black wattle, Acacia mearnsii, not Mimosa tenuiflora. The two are different plants from different continents. When a supplier sells Mimosa hostilis root bark, as we do, it is the root bark of Mimosa tenuiflora; check the botanical name before you buy, because black wattle bark will not give the same colors.
## Which should you buy?

- **For pinks, plums and burgundy:** Mimosa hostilis root bark.
- **For dependable warm browns:** cutch.
- **For red-browns and heavy leather work:** quebracho.
- **To prepare cotton and linen for any dye:** oak gall, then alum.
- **For greys and near-blacks:** any of them with iron, with Mimosa hostilis giving the coolest slate.

Many dyers keep Mimosa hostilis for color and a gall or tannin mordant for plant fibers. [Wool, silk, cotton and linen in the same bath](/blog/wool-silk-cotton-and-linen-in-the-same-bath) shows how that pairing works in one pot.
